Honestly, I didn't expect to enjoy this entry as much as I did.
Coming from Civ 5, I initially found the art style, character designs, and UI a bit off-putting, especially considering how charming Civ 5's presentation was. However, they gradually grow on you, and the game starts to feel more beginner-friendly, with each branch of progression,Units,buildingsmechanics being relatively easier to identify and navigate.
There are also more varied interactions and unique mechanics for each civilization, which was one of my biggest complaints about Civ 5. On top of that, you have more unique actions available for different units and buildings or Civ, which helps break up the tedious cycle of "press next turn until you can actually do something."
What I appreciate the most, though, are the quotes that accompany technology unlocks. They feel much more noticeable and memorable than they did in Civ 5. But the music felt a bit on the weaker side maybe i was not paying attention to it as much. The game rules and modifiers are also a welcome addition, as they introduce some much-needed chaos and variety.

The most annoying mechanic I've encountered so far is the World Council, which becomes available quite early but has barely any noticeable impact until around the midgame and the global warming mechanic with the floods but the natural disasters and zombies are quite funny. The map generation also feels somewhat lacking but as usual, mods can fix most of these complaints, and some of them introduce much-desired QoL improvements. I hope the developers take note and implement some of these features in their future games. It seems to be a recurring pattern where they overlook certain UI elements or fail to provide enough context on how particular mechanics are can to work.

What I love most about Civ VI is the amount of control and meaningful decisions it gives me. I enjoy expanding aggressively in the early game, securing territory, building defensible borders and preparing for potential wars. Then comes my favorite part: developing those settlements into powerful, specialized cities while carefully balancing food, production, gold, science and culture.

Managing builders, assigning citizens to specific tiles, planning districts and optimizing individual cities might seem like unnecessary micromanagement to some, but to me, that's the heart of Civilization. Every little decision contributes to something bigger. You're not just watching an empire grow; you're building it yourself. The real enjoyment comes from developing an empire and competing with other civilizations throughout history.

Civ VI wasn't perfect at launch. I initially found its art style a little goofy, and I believe some of the content introduced through expansions should have been part of the base game. I'm not a fan of games relying on paid DLC to feel complete. However, Rise and Fall and Gathering Storm helped turn an already enjoyable game into something truly exceptional.

Playing Civilization VII has actually made me appreciate Civ VI even more. While VII introduces some interesting ideas, I feel that too many meaningful decisions have been simplified, automated or removed entirely. Losing builders, manual tile management and much of the freedom I had when developing my empire has reminded me why I enjoyed the previous games so much.

I don't need a Civilization game to be more complicated just for the sake of complexity. I want the freedom to make meaningful decisions and experience the consequences of those decisions throughout thousands of years of history. 

That's what Civilization VI does so well!!
It's not about winning as quickly as possible. It's about taking a single settler, founding a civilization, shaping its history and eventually looking across the map at an empire that exists because of the choices you made.

Civilization VI isn't perfect, but it's a fantastic strategy game, and one I can happily spend another thousand hours playing.

This is a great time sink but honestly it takes too much time. I remember when I could play Civ 1 and complete a game in a few hours, and depending on your start point, sometimes within 30 minutes. With Civ 6 it takes days/hours. There are no "quick" games, even when you select quick. I like to be left alone when I play but with this version, there must be at least 7 or so other civs, which is a lot to me. I tried choosing XL North America map and that isn't helpful because it'll plop another civ right next to me. The barbarians are also pretty advanced as compared to civ progression. You have to be very careful or you can be one-shot if you just let your character auto-explore.

Can we talk about how auto-explore is the best thing ever added to Civ over the years?

All this to say, I have still played it for 82 hours so far and I'll play it again tomorrow. I have Civ 7 on Switch 2, which I need to go back to now that I've played this one more. Civ 1 is still my favorite haha.

Even ten years later, core conflicts in the game are not fixed. Diplomacy is entirely useless and the best way to do it is just to ignore it entirely. Districts and wonders taking up entire tiles breaks your ability to play tall or on islands. 

This seems like a minor problem, but it is particularly egregious when you consider that they made poorly planned choices such as Kupe; He is an oceanic-spawning leader that is typically found on small islands, whose ability requires leaving nature untouched. In previous games where your city only took up one tile, this was possible. But with the way that Civ 6 works, his ability works directly against itself and the mechanics of the game. 

Diplomacy just straight up doesn't work. The game will ignore it's own systems, and it does not track very basic concepts like "you have to survive to win the game". The AI will literally refuse to hand over diplomatic favour points in order to keep playing, and choose instead to die.

The AI for units also doesn't exist. They just wander about randomly on their own, there is absolutely no central command script, and they are useless. If you ever wonder why the enemy infantry gets in the way of their own siege units from reaching your city, it's because they literally are not co-ordinated in any way.

There are so many of these issues in the game, it's clear that nobody was talking to each other when they made it. On their own they sound like okay ideas, but put together they make each other actively worse.

Without a doubt one of the greatest strategy games ever made with addicting gameplay, variety, and a contender for the best OST ever composed. Easy to learn, hard to master. Each mechanic, improvement, wonder, leader, etc. supports each other and builds up the game to create a ridiculous (but not overcomplicated) level of depth and replayability. Everything here just clicks perfectly. 

I love every part of this game, but I think the music takes the cake. So much effort went into bringing all these vibrant cultures to life and it's reflected perfectly in the soundtrack. Each civilization's individual theme was handled with an unbelievable level of care and precision that it's frankly staggering. Without the OST this game would be half of what it is today, and It has personally affected me beyond words. Thank you Geoff Knorr, Roland Rizzo, Griffin Cohen, Phill Boucher, and Christopher Tin for your service to the world.

Now that the joke is over, the game is only worth it if you buy the Anthology pack. The Anthology pack includes all the expansions necessary to mod the hell out of the game and it also allows you to play with interesting Civs and game modes; the game is a little boring if you don't play with Rise and Fall or Gathering Storm. 
I usually run between 150 to 200 mods, UI mods are necessary (map tacks, simple UI adjustments, extended policies, etc) but other mods are optional if recommended (from aesthetic mods like Colder tundra, to entire Civilizations like Sukritact's Siam) . 
Here is a list of good modders, if it's made by them the mod is usually really good: Sukritact (the best modder out there, with mods like Sukritact's Oceans and lots of Civ changes/new civs), JNR (interesting terrain mods and new mechanics), Leugi and Pokiehl.
